title: Why Spaghetti Never Snaps in Two #science #physics
description:
Try to snap a long, dry spaghetti strand in two by bending it. You almost never can: it usually breaks into three or more pieces. In slow motion, the first break makes the pieces snap back, and that sends a bending wave down the strand that breaks it again. Researchers at MIT found a fix: twist the strand almost a full turn first, then bend it slowly. Now it usually snaps in two. It takes a few tries by hand.

More slow-motion surprises: Why do wheels spin backwards on camera? https://youtu.be/SxjS9sdc_Ek

Sources
- Audoly and Neukirch, Fragmentation of rods by cascading cracks: why spaghetti does not break in half, Physical Review Letters 95, 095505 (2005)
- Heisser, Patil, Dunkel, Brun, Audoly et al., Controlling fracture cascades through twisting and quenching, PNAS (2018); arXiv 1802.05402
- MIT News, MIT mathematicians solve age-old spaghetti mystery (news.mit.edu, 2018-08-13)
- The strand is drawn much thicker than real spaghetti, and the wave is schematic

Try it: how many tries did it take you to get two pieces?

Script, voice and animation are AI-produced (Claude; Kokoro voice). Every claim is checked against the sources above.
